items.title: The new human-crafted Apple Music brand matters in an AI world
items.summary: Apple has introduced a new Liquid Glass design identity for Apple Music that emphasizes human-crafted aesthetics. The author reflects on the shift in design language and the broader implications of human creativity in an increasingly AI-driven world.
items.content:
Apple just revealed a new brand identity for Apple Music, with the expected turn to Liquid Glass. I’m not much of a fan of their new design language in general; this is where I admit that I’m still running MacOS Sequoia and have grumpy things to say about rounded corner radii and text legibility.

It’s just a trend, it will pass, and at some point I’ll probably cave and upgrade when it starts actually affecting my ability to get work done, or more importantly get security updates. Once I adjust, I’ll stop noticing it, and life will go on.

As such, I wouldn’t normally find an obvious rebrand like this notable, much less feel like I had much to say about it. But then I happened to catch Apple’s behind-the-scenes video in my YouTube recommendations, and I realized I did have thoughts.

items.title: OpenAI's latest AI models are coming to Google Cloud and Antigravity
items.summary: OpenAI's latest GPT models are coming to Google Cloud's Model Garden to expand enterprise options. The integration will also bring these models to Google's agent-powered coding tool, Antigravity.
items.content:
Google would certainly prefer that everyone used its Gemini models with Google Cloud services, but soon, you'll have more options. OpenAI and Google have come to an arrangement that will see the former's frontier models arrive in Google Cloud services. Perhaps more importantly, GPT models will soon appear in Antigravity, Google's agent-powered coding tool.

For enterprise customers and AI enthusiasts, OpenAI's latest model will appear in Google's "Model Garden" in the coming weeks, adding to its 200-plus options. The garden already offers access to Google's Gemini models, as well as an assortment of open models like Mistral, Llama, and Gemma. Anthropic's Claude AI has also been available for some time. Google says it's now the only large cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed LLMs.

While OpenAI notes that Microsoft continues to be its primary cloud partner, the full suite of current GPT 6 and 6.1 models—Astra, Sol, and Luna—will launch on Google Cloud. Astra will naturally cost the most to run, but Google's system supports dynamically moving workloads between LLMs based on performance, latency, and efficiency.

items.title: Judge rejects Trump’s wild claim EPA can dismiss data center pollution lawsuits
items.summary: A judge rejected Donald Trump's attempt to grant the EPA unilateral authority to dismiss Clean Air Act lawsuits against SpaceXAI. The ruling allows the NAACP's case regarding pollution from a Memphis data center to proceed.
items.content:
Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI is stuck facing a lawsuit over alleged data center pollution after Donald Trump failed to convince a judge that his Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has complete control over all Clean Air Act lawsuits and can dismiss any suit at whim.

Soon after unpermitted gas turbines were discovered powering Musk’s giant Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee, the NAACP sued. Its lawsuit sought an injunction requiring xAI (which, following a merger, is known now as SpaceXAI) to use the best available pollution control technology when operating the turbines and ordering penalties up to $124,426 per day per violation. Without such remedies, the turbines risked drastically spiking pollution in already vulnerable neighborhoods housing predominantly Black communities nearby, the NAACP argued.

To block the lawsuit, Trump tried to intervene, arguing that the EPA had the power to unilaterally dismiss lawsuits any time the president decides against enforcing the Clean Air Act. According to Trump, it would supposedly “not serve the public interest” if citizens were allowed to seek massive civil penalties to punish polluting AI firms that were trying to get data centers operational as fast as possible to support Trump’s AI Action Plan.

items.title: The $15 billion ad-powered AI startup your doctor may already be using
items.summary: OpenEvidence has reached a $15 billion valuation as its ad-powered AI search engine becomes a primary tool for two-thirds of US doctors. The platform assists physicians in diagnosing and treating patients by rapidly analyzing vast amounts of medical literature and clinical guidelines.
items.content:
Nearly two-thirds of US doctors are turning to an AI-powered search engine to make patient decisions, propelling a little-known tech startup to a $15 billion valuation while prompting a debate over the future of patient care.

Miami-based OpenEvidence, founded by serial entrepreneur Daniel Nadler in 2022, said that many of America’s 1 million physicians processed more than 42 million prompts last month. Doctors are using the company’s chatbot to scour medical journals and clinical guidelines to help diagnose and treat patients.

The ads-powered platform has grown largely by word of mouth, penetrating a sector where few tools have seen similar traction. “We’re the first viral consumer internet app in healthcare,” Nadler told the FT in an interview.

items.title: VentureBeat names Rob Strechay as its first Lead Analyst, expanding its enterprise AI research push
items.summary: VentureBeat has appointed Rob Strechay as its first Lead Analyst to spearhead the launch of VentureBeat Research. This strategic move aims to provide specialized enterprise AI insights tailored for technical decision-makers and executives.
items.content:
Rob Strechay, until recently managing director and principal analyst at theCUBE Research, has joined VentureBeat as our first Lead Analyst and a founding analyst of VentureBeat Research. His arrival is the next step in a deliberate move at VentureBeat toward deeper specialization: analysis built for the technical decision-makers — the directors, VPs, CIOs, and CTOs — who are evaluating, buying, and deploying enterprise AI.

items.title: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam
items.summary: Epic Games has released a preview of its new launcher, which was rebuilt from scratch using AI-assisted coding to improve speed and responsiveness. The company claims this new version is significantly faster than its predecessor and will support Windows, Mac, and Linux.
items.content:
Nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own Game Store and launcher, the Fortnite maker is deploying a new tool to give it an edge over Valve: vibe coding.

In announcing the new publicly available "Preview" build of its Epic Games Launcher, Epic writes that "programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look." And while that might sound a little tongue-in-cheek, Epic Games Store General Manager and VP Martin Keely told PC Gamer that the team "started from scratch" and used AI as "a tool to write and review new features and new capabilities from the ground up in a different tech stack than what we had previously." The goal, Keely said, was to "look at functionality that existed [in the current Epic Games Launcher] and [say] we want to replicate that, but not the code itself."

Speaking to IGN, Keely clarified that using AI to code the new Launcher "made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms, support Windows and Mac, and we're going to have a Linux version as well."

items.title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
items.summary: Researchers have utilized AI-based design tools to engineer custom enzymes capable of breaking down specific proteins. This breakthrough demonstrates potential for targeting proteins linked to various neurological diseases.
items.content:
A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment.

Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases.

Cutting proteins
The basic peptide bond isn't especially interesting-looking—it's what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.)

items.title: Recording device hidden in toilet paper found in top-secret OpenAI meeting room
items.summary: An OpenAI engineer was arrested for allegedly planting a hidden recording device in a restricted executive conference room to steal trade secrets. The FBI claims the suspect attempted to retrieve the device after it was discovered by company security.
items.content:
It took OpenAI two days to notice that a recording device was hidden in a restricted executive conference room where leadership met to discuss highly confidential information, including technical progress, government engagements, and commercial partnerships.

Only those with special clearance are supposed to access that room. But the FBI believes the recording device was planted by Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer from Saudi Arabia, who became a permanent US legal resident in 2020. In a press release Tuesday announcing his arrest, the FBI alleged that chatbot logs and CCTV footage suggested that Alfozan—who worked as an OpenAI engineer for more than a year—sought to use the device to spy on OpenAI and risked leaking trade secrets in a way that threatened national security.

To conceal the USB device, Alfozan allegedly wrapped it in toilet paper, then plugged it into the back of a conference room television. The device was likely planted on September 28, and OpenAI found it on September 30 and quickly determined that its contents were encrypted, the FBI said. Days later, on October 5, OpenAI installed a camera in that conference room, and the CCTV footage allegedly showed Alfozan attempting to retrieve the recording device that same day.

items.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
items.summary: Anthropic warns that emerging small AI models could enable self-replicating malware capable of autonomously infecting IoT devices. These AI-driven worms would be difficult to neutralize because they lack a centralized control point and can adapt to unfamiliar hardware.
items.content:
AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown.

By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms.

Challenging to shut down
Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.”

items.title: OpenAI, Google pushing new AI models easily tricked into making nudes, researchers say
items.summary: Researchers warn that leading AI image generators from OpenAI and Google are increasingly susceptible to producing non-consensual explicit content. Despite the growing threat, current safety measures are failing to effectively prevent the creation of these harmful deepfakes.
items.content:
Safety researchers continue to warn that a large volume of AI-generated explicit content is spreading unchecked, while regulators do little to meaningfully stop it.

This non-consensual content is commonly shared in text and direct messages or stored in private clouds where it’s less likely to be detected or reported, a Google co-authored study of Internet users across the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom found this July. That’s why the “most critical intervention point” remains at the source: the harmful AI tools used to make the fake sexual images, Google researchers concluded.

Yet red-teaming in recent months suggests that as some of the leading AI image generators from Google and OpenAI become more capable, they may be getting worse at blocking explicit outputs.

items.title: Meta drops the word "train" from its commercial TOS after AI backlash
items.summary: Meta removed the word 'train' from its upcoming commercial terms of service following public backlash regarding data scraping concerns. The company updated the policy without notifying users, leaving experts skeptical about how business page data will be utilized.
items.content:
Hoping to quell criticism, Meta has dropped the word “train” from its “streamlined” commercial terms of service that kick in on October 30.

Last week, Meta faced backlash after legal experts warned that the tech giant’s sweeping new commercial terms of service seemed to give Meta permission to endlessly scrape websites linked on business pages. Talking to Nieman Lab, experts suggested that Meta could possibly use the policy to avoid millions in licensing fees from news organizations by requiring all business users to share a wealth of AI training data simply for running a business page.

A Meta spokesperson confirmed that Meta did not alert users to the changed language following backlash. This potentially only adds to confusion ahead of the policy rollout. In response to backlash, Meta's spokesperson provided a statement to Ars, acknowledging Nieman Lab's initial report but not its follow-up report reiterating experts' concerns:

items.title: Gemini's Personal Intelligence is coming to cars
items.summary: Google is expanding its Gemini Personal Intelligence feature to Android Auto and vehicles with Google built-in. This update allows the AI to provide more context-aware responses by accessing personal data from apps like Gmail and Calendar.
items.content:
Google kicked off 2026 with the addition of Personal Intelligence to Gemini, allowing its AI to pull in more of your data to formulate answers. It started as a paid feature but eventually came to all Gemini users. However, this feature wasn't available in the car until now. Google is rolling out Personal Intelligence to Android Auto and Google Built-in, and it is still, thankfully, an optional feature.

As Google points out, a generative AI's outputs are better "when it knows the world and knows you," which is correct in an uncomfortable sort of way. The more context you can provide to a model, the better the output will be at the end of the token shuffle. Since Google has so much of your data already, it sees Personal Intelligence as a differentiator versus other AI systems. You don't have to provide the AI context because it already has it from apps like Gmail and Calendar.

Personal Intelligence is beginning its rollout in Android Auto today, and it will come to vehicles with Google built-in in the next few months. As an aside, "Google built-in" is questionable branding, but it refers to cars that run Google software in the infotainment system rather than projecting an interface from your phone. Very few vehicles have Google built-in, but Google often releases new car features on them first. This time, it's the other way around.

items.title: Ukraine’s drone rescue of wounded soldier puts much touted idea into practice
items.summary: Ukraine successfully conducted its first battlefield drone evacuation of a wounded soldier using a heavy-lift hexacopter. This operation marks a significant advancement in military technology, moving beyond experimental concepts into practical frontline application.
items.content:
Ukraine’s unprecedented drone rescue of a wounded soldier from the battlefield has shown once again how battlefield necessity can spur innovation. The operation was revealed just days after separate Ukrainian drones designed for casualty evacuation were deployed for frontline testing—taking a step beyond the US military’s decades of experimentation with similar concepts.

The drone evacuation of the injured soldier took place at an undisclosed time and place on the frontline where the presence of Russian drones and landmines made it impractical to send in a wheeled ground robot, according to The Kyiv Independent. On October 19, Ukraine’s Army shared a video of the drone evacuation, showing the wounded soldier securing himself in a harness suspended beneath a heavy hexacopter drone with six rotors before being flown to safety.

“This is a historic event, the next stage of evacuating the wounded, which we will all come to,” said Napalm, a programmer of the 92nd separate assault brigade's unmanned ground systems company, who went by his callsign per Ukrainian military practice, in a statement. “Now the serious systematic work begins, so that such missions are carried out constantly.”

items.title: Meta tries to scapegoat staff who downloaded torrents to spare execs
items.summary: A judge has ordered Meta to identify the executives who authorized the use of pirated books from shadow libraries for AI training. The company previously attempted to deflect blame onto individual staff members by claiming the data collection process lacked formal leadership oversight.
items.content:
In copyright lawsuits over AI training, Meta has spent weeks blaming staff for downloading torrents. The company has now been ordered to name executives who authorized decisions to pirate books from shadow libraries like Anna’s Archive and LibGen, TorrentFreak reported.

In a discovery order impacting a class action raised by book authors—including Richard Kadrey and Sarah Silverman—as well as a lawsuit from publisher Entrepreneur Media, Magistrate Judge Thomas Hixon largely agreed that Meta must clearly identify key decision-makers. Following testimony from Meta staff who downloaded torrents, the order could expose a wider range of supervisors, managers, and executives whom staffers said greenlit the piracy.

Meta had been hoping to avoid detailing the chain of command, particularly for leadership involved in early AI training. According to a Meta court filing, its initial efforts to compile massive AI datasets were managed through an “informal approach" where supposedly nobody with authority made any decisions. Instead, Meta insisted that a “decision” was “made only in the sense” that some staffers “technically” downloaded torrents.

items.title: The new economics of enterprise AI
items.summary: Enterprise AI is shifting from experimental use cases to foundational infrastructure, requiring a transition from tracking raw GPU costs to measuring the effective cost per useful business outcome. Organizations must move beyond simple infrastructure ownership toward operational discipline, utilizing integrated platforms to optimize model selection, scheduling, and resource efficiency.
items.content:
Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from “can we use it?” to “how efficiently are we using it?”

Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes.

That’s the metric worth tracking: effective cost per useful outcome — the total platform, model, operations, and capacity cost required to complete work the business can actually use, whether a resolved request or a completed workflow.

Three ways to run AI

Utilization is central to the economics. Directing more work to paid-for capacity lowers effective unit cost; idle GPUs, fragmented workloads, and oversized models all raise the cost of every useful result. Enterprises generally choose among three models:

A bespoke stack — procuring infrastructure and controls in-house. This approach is flexible, but it creates a continuing burden, since teams must revalidate the environment as models and policies change.

On-demand consumption — hyperscalers reduce the assembly burden and suit low or uncertain demand, but charges rise with every prompt or agent action.

An integrated private AI platform — owned or dedicated capacity paired with a validated stack. The advantage isn’t free inference; it’s control over efficiency levers like scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management.

The right model depends on the workload. APIs can be rational for experimentation or variable demand. As workloads become sustained and business-critical, enterprises need to weigh not just what they consume, but how efficiently they operate the system.

Ownership is an operating discipline

Buying a Formula 1 race car and parking it in your garage means owning one of the most sophisticated vehicles ever built — but ownership alone doesn’t make you competitive; you still need drivers, mechanics, and track time to justify it. AI infrastructure works the same way.

One of the biggest misconceptions in enterprise AI is that owning infrastructure automatically improves economics. Owning GPUs creates the opportunity for better economics, but only if the organization has sufficient demand and operational discipline to keep resources productive.

The infrastructure that returns the best ROI isn’t a reference architecture or a bespoke build-out — it’s a fully integrated, qualified stack that lets teams route tasks to the least costly model that meets quality requirements and reuse context through techniques such as KV-cache management, reducing wasted capacity while maintaining responsiveness.

Without these practices, committed infrastructure can become stranded capital. With them, rising demand improves economics as fixed costs are amortized across more useful work — increasingly important in agentic systems, where economics are shaped less by any single prompt than by the efficiency of the complete environment.

From deployment to value

HPE Private Cloud AI is a production-ready foundation combining infrastructure, software, models, tools, governance, and services, reducing the integration burden of operating private AI at scale. Its architecture lets teams manage scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management as operational levers, aligning capacity and service levels with each workload’s requirements. It also includes a 90-day engagement with forward-deployed engineers who help customer teams deploy initial use cases and establish repeatable operating practices.

In independent testing commissioned by HPE, an integrated platform serving multiple workloads at high utilization delivered a lower effective cost per token than repeatedly renting equivalent capacity. Actual results will vary based on workload mix and utilization.

Measure what matters

Token consumption remains useful, but it isn’t a complete measure of AI economics. A fuller enterprise view tracks cost per business-relevant outcome, accelerator utilization, and model choice relative to task complexity.

Enterprises already operating private AI should ask how mature their utilization is, and how workload volume will change over the next 12 to 18 months. Those earlier in the journey should build these practices in from the first deployment, so strategy anticipates growth before demand becomes a bottleneck.

For low-volume, unpredictable demand, an API or hyperscaler may remain sensible. But as AI becomes a continuous production capability, enterprises have a growing incentive to control utilization, amortize fixed costs, and manage the environment as a long-term operating asset. The strategic question isn’t whether enterprises will pay for AI — it’s whether they will understand, and ultimately own, the economics behind it.

items.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
items.summary: Researchers discovered that Meta's Muse AI exposes sensitive user conversations through easily discoverable shared links. Despite Meta's privacy claims, the platform's URL generation method allows unauthorized access to private personal and business data.
items.content:
Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through Web links, researchers reported Monday.

Like many online services, Muse allows users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.

A single query is all that's required

Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including:

items.title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
items.summary: While the tech sector currently leads in AI integration, other industries like finance and healthcare are following a predictable adoption curve as they automate workflows. Employees who proactively learn to validate AI outputs and streamline administrative tasks gain significant professional leverage and influence over company policy.
items.content:
The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line.

As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn’t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie.

The AI adoption spectrum by industry

Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy (see Figure 1).

Figure 1: The AI adoption curve remains steep across industries, but non-tech industry adoption rates are increasing.

Source: TripleTen, 2026

While tech leads the way, finance emerges as a clear second: 48% of finance workers have been asked to use AI chatbots, and 32% have been asked to automate parts of their workflow. This demonstrates how rapidly knowledge work integrates AI once clear use cases emerge. 

By contrast, sectors like healthcare (18% asked to use chatbots) and education (25%) reflect lower initial exposure. Because these broad industry categories encompass a mix of specialized hands-on professionals, clinical or instructional personnel, and back-office administrative staff, universal adoption was never going to happen overnight. Integrating automated tools into compliance-heavy or human-facing operations requires a more deliberate pace, which is reflected by the lower numbers.

The AI skills workers are being asked to learn 

Across all surveyed industries, 79% of workers report being asked to learn at least one skill they didn’t previously have. Looking at the specific competencies demanded in tech today offers a preview of the skill sets likely to shift into other sectors (see Figure 2).

Figure 2: Workforces across industries are learning new skills.

Source: TripleTen, 2026

Although some of these sound like niche skills confined to tech, many of them will translate to frontline work across sectors—from hospital systems managing patient logistics to school districts processing administrative reporting. 

One skill gets less attention than it should. Only 30% of managers and owners call judging whether AI output is right or wrong an absolute must, which puts it sixth on a list of seven. As AI tools reach more industries, this is the skill that catches mistakes before they cause problems. It is also where work experience helps most: To spot a wrong answer, you need to know what the right one looks like.

How early AI adoption helps your career

Early AI adoption offers clear professional leverage: TripleTen’s survey data shows that when managers learned a new skill or automation process from an employee, 88% of those employee-led AI innovations became standard company practice.

In early-adopting industries, employees who identify repetitive administrative tasks and use AI tools to streamline them have a voice in shaping organizational policy. As healthcare networks, educational institutions, and retail operations begin broader rollouts of AI-enabled software, workers who understand how to validate outputs, prompt models, and automate routine tasks will hold a strong advantage. Being the person who can streamline administrative overhead promises better chances for retention, promotions, and wage growth. 

Ana Riabova, the AI strategy and enablement lead at TripleTen, says, “Everyone talks about saving time, but the real win with early adoption is expanding what you can actually do. People who get ahead are using it to handle things they used to have to hand off. It doesn’t matter how senior or junior you are. You keep your core skills, but suddenly you aren’t boxed in by them anymore.”

The AI resource gap: Who pays for training and how workers learn

If non-tech industries absorb these tools more gradually, the challenge for workers lies in getting access to quality learning resources. Workers’ out-of-pocket investment in training varies significantly by industry:

Tech: $1,758 average (13% spent $0)

Finance: $1,664 average (24% spent $0)

Healthcare: $990 average (45% spent $0)

Education: $883 average (42% spent $0)

Nearly half of healthcare and education workers spent nothing out of pocket on professional development last year. Furthermore, tech workers actively leverage a larger variety of learning channels (see Figure 3).

Figure 3: Professional development efforts mirror the AI adoption curve.

Source: TripleTen, 2026

Tech workers are nearly twice as likely as all workers to use AI chatbots as learning tools (48% vs. 27%), and more than twice as likely as workers outside tech (21%), effectively using AI to accelerate their acquisition of other skills. 

However, ask workers whom they trust most to teach them a new job skill, and they choose someone currently doing that job (31%). Fewer pick an official certification program (19%), an AI tool (16%), or a university professor (6%).

Conclusion

The difference in AI adoption rates across industries is not a story of who is succeeding and who is failing. Rather, it’s a timeline of how technology diffuses through an economy. Tech and finance are testing the mechanics of AI integration today. For workers in healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing, the current phase provides a valuable window to observe which skills generate real productivity gains—allowing them to build those competencies before they become standard industry expectations.

This content was produced by TripleTen. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

items.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
items.summary: Samsung is rapidly expanding its massive semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek to meet the surging global demand for AI-focused memory chips. The site operates around the clock as the company strives to regain its competitive edge against rivals like SK Hynix.
items.content:
_____________

THE PLACE

Pyeongtaek,

South Korea

Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring.

It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. 

They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes. 

In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. 

Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. 

Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. 

Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.”

items.title: Google just redesigned the search box for the first time in 25 years — here’s why it matters more than you think.
items.summary: Google is officially retiring its iconic search box interface after 25 years of service. This redesign marks a fundamental shift in how users interact with the search engine's results.
items.content:
For a quarter century, the Google search box has been one of the most recognizable interfaces in computing: a thin white rectangle, a blinking cursor, a few typed words, and a list of blue links. On Tuesday, Google will formally retire that paradigm.

Read more

items.title: Disney offers $20M for Character.AI’s scandal-plagued chatbot tech
items.summary: Disney has offered $20 million for a non-exclusive license to Character.AI's chatbot technology despite previously criticizing the company for intellectual property theft. This move marks a significant shift in strategy following Disney's earlier legal threats regarding the misuse of its brand assets.
items.content:
In a bankruptcy proceeding that kicked off yesterday, Disney has offered to buy some of the technology that powers the controversy-plagued chatbot Character.AI.

Disney is willing to pay $20 million for “a non-exclusive perpetual license” of certain Character Technologies intellectual property, the chatbot maker said in a press release that did not go into much further detail on which assets Disney wanted.

The move may be surprising. In September 2025, Disney joined others in publicly criticizing Character.AI for stealing content and harming kids. Specifically, Disney sent a strongly worded cease-and-desist letter that accused Character Technologies of weaponizing Disney characters “in a way that could damage its brand long term,” Axios reported.

items.title: Google wants to host your personal vibe-coded apps in the Play Store
items.summary: Google is expanding its AI-powered discovery tools in the Play Store with enhanced search features and a new personalized game recommendation engine. The company also plans to introduce a private hosting platform for users to share their own AI-generated applications.
items.content:
Google has already added a few AI features to the Play Store, but a lot more are coming. The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google's app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder. For people who have embraced AI to build their own apps, the Play Store will soon offer a way to privately host and share those creations.

Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon.

Google's other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google's app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA.

items.title: Gemini 4 Argon begins rolling out in Gemini app and Antigravity, but only if you pay
items.summary: Google has begun rolling out its advanced Gemini 4 Argon model to paying subscribers after initial safety concerns. The model demonstrates high-level reasoning and coding capabilities, already proving effective in optimizing internal Google systems and robotics projects.
items.content:
Google revealed Gemini 4 Argon a few weeks ago, saying that it needed to move cautiously toward a full release because of the potential for nefarious use. Google seems to have worked all that out pretty quickly, though. Argon is beginning its wide rollout today, but it's only coming to paying users at this time, and even those on lower-tier plans won't have full access.

Nothing about Gemini 4 Argon's capabilities has changed. Google still points to the benchmarks it published late last month as evidence of the model's advanced reasoning and agentic coding capabilities. The model is supposedly trained to refuse malicious instructions, and an automated misalignment monitor can stop processing if it detects an unintended workflow. Google claims Argon needs that because it's so capable.

The company has a few new examples of how Argon has helped inside Google, where it has been used by thousands of Googlers. Argon has reportedly been instrumental in making YouTube's comment system more efficient. Argon identified redundant emoji rendering that, when eliminated, dropped server load by 45 percent. Engineers also turned Gemini 4 loose on the proprietary drone physics simulator used in Project Wing, and the AI found critical bugs that had been in the codebase since 2018. Google also notes that Argon has advanced its robotics program, showing a measurable step increase in embodied reasoning.

items.title: They war-gamed dimming the Sun. It went even worse than you think.
items.summary: Experts participated in a war-game simulation to explore the geopolitical risks and governance challenges of solar geoengineering technologies. The exercise revealed that achieving international consensus on ethical research and deployment is significantly more difficult than researchers initially anticipated.
items.content:
When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.

“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it's for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”

The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.

items.title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
items.summary: The debate over open-source AI models centers on balancing the risks of misuse by bad actors against the benefits of democratization and research transparency. While closed models currently lead in performance, open models offer greater control, lower costs, and essential access for academic study.
items.content:
MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.

Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs. 

These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models.

“I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely.

There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth.

What are the benefits of open models?

Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available. 

Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so. 

If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications.

Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla. And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure.

But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.”

Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it.

Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience.

But open models are no

items.title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
items.summary: AI labs are increasingly purchasing data archives from defunct startups to overcome the limitations of public and synthetic training datasets. While these transactions provide a new revenue stream for failing companies, they raise significant legal and privacy concerns regarding the handling of sensitive employee information.
items.content:
When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says.

The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. 

SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. 

And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.” 

Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined.

Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code.

That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data, including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. 

Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use.

There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker, this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales.

While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left. 

Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

items.title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
items.summary: While AI infrastructure planning often focuses on expensive GPU compute, the hidden costs of storing massive amounts of inference-generated data are rapidly outpacing budgets. Organizations must now account for the long-term storage footprint of AI outputs, which requires a strategic balance between high-performance access and cost-effective capacity.
items.content:
Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs.

What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning.

As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it

Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind.

Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. That’s a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw. Scale this to an enterprise generating longer, higher resolution video and the back-end footprint grows into the hundreds of gigabytes per clip.

And that back-end footprint is growing fast. McKinsey projects AI inference demand will grow at a 35% CAGR through 2030, versus 22% for training, making up more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade.

A recent WD-sponsored IDC global white paper that surveyed 763 IT and business decision makers found that nearly 95% of respondents reported an increase in data volume due to generative AI over the past 12 months, with roughly 61% reporting growth of 25% or more.

“You can think of having more storage as an optimization for keeping the GPUs busy,” said a senior product manager of a hyperscale cloud service provider quoted in report. “The biggest challenge is to ensure that the GPUs are not idle, waiting for data to show up—hours of GPU idle time becomes very expensive, very fast.” Put in dollar terms: if your storage spend is growing 25% year over year while your compute budget grows in the more predictable cyclical way, storage ends up outpacing the budget line that receives the most attention.

Matching storage to the AI data life cycle

Compute demand rises and falls with training cycles, product launches, and hardware refreshes. But the volume of retained data doesn’t fall back down with it when compute demand slows. Model logs, synthetic outputs, inference results, and more keep accumulating, and organizations are holding onto more of it for longer.

This changes the role of retained data. Information that once moved into an archive and rarely surfaced can now become an input to future AI workloads. As more data is retained, retrieved, and reused, storage must support not only growing capacity, but increasingly dynamic access to it. The same WD-IDC survey found 96% of respondents anticipate needing faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

AI workloads require both performance and capacity, with different technologies serving different needs across the data lifecycle. And for the vast volumes of data that must be retained and revisited, HDDs provide a cost-effective, high-capacity foundation, with a significant cost-per-terabyte advantage  

What this means for how AI gets budgeted

For a CFO or CIO, this means “AI infrastructure spend” may be scoped too narrowly on compute. A model that idles while data loads costs about as much as one idling for lack of a GPU. But the storage bottleneck stays hidden until it’s already a problem, surfacing in operating costs and retrieval delays rather than a CapEx line next to the accelerators.

Consider a retailer generating AI product videos for its catalog, or an insurer running claims documents through a RAG pipeline for faster underwriting. In both cases, the compute cost is a known, budgeted quantity: a per-generation or per-query rate that finance can forecast. The storage cost is different: It compounds with every video generated and every claim processed, because none of that back-end data disappears once the task is finished.

A team that budgets AI as “compute plus a rounding error for storage” may find, in 12 to 18 months, that the rounding error has become a significant fraction of the program’s total cost—right around the time leadership is deciding whether to expand.

Building for economically scalable capacity

Addressing this challenge starts with architecture. Storage strategy tends to be designed for expensive, hot-tier performance (for data accessed instantly and constantly), while most AI data by volume accumulates in the warm, cool, and cold tiers behind it.

What enterprises need is economically scalable capacity: Infrastructure designed for the full AI data life cycle, balancing performance with capacity, power, reliability, and total cost of ownership as data persists, compounds, and is increasingly reused. That means treating archives that once sat untouched as active assets for RAG and inference, and setting retention policies for data’s growing strategic value rather than its original storage cost. It also means recognizing that decisions about storage play out across fleets, not individual drives.

Such infrastructure requires storage tiers, where individualized power consumption, reliability, density, and operational efficiency all determine whether the system remains economically sustainable as capacity scales.

What’s our data retention policy for AI-generat

items.title: Report: FTC probes Anthropic, OpenAI after Trump dismissed AI fears as “hoax”
items.summary: The FTC has launched an investigation into Anthropic and OpenAI regarding potential consumer harms and recent AI security breaches. The agency is demanding extensive documentation on internal safety protocols and marketing practices following reports of AI models compromising government systems.
items.content:
Following a string of incidents where AI models hacked websites and breached government systems during testing phases, the Federal Trade Commission is officially probing Anthropic and OpenAI over consumer harms, an insider told Axios.

On Wednesday, the FTC sent out civil investigative demands seeking a wide range of information from the AI firms on recent safety incidents.

The FTC did not respond to Ars’ request to review the subpoena demands. However, Axios’ source said the requests spanned more than 50 pages of questions and sought documents related to the incidents, internal security measures taken, and marketing materials that may suggest consumers were misled.

items.title: Singer or clanker? YouTube Music will tell you with new gen AI labeling.
items.summary: YouTube Music is introducing new labels to identify tracks created using generative AI tools. This initiative aims to provide transparency for listeners while acknowledging the evolving role of AI in music production.
items.content:
Genuine human creativity takes time, but you know what doesn't? AI slop. There are countless AI models out there that can make something that passes for music, and you might come across those tracks on streaming services without realizing it. Google says it will begin labeling that content in YouTube Music, building on similar disclosures in the main YouTube app.

Google is not outright banning AI music or even speaking ill of it. "Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music," the company says in a blog post.

However, the company also acknowledges that people want to know if a song was created with generative AI tools. A new label for AI content on YouTube Music is now rolling out in the app and on the website, which looks a lot like a label Google began adding to AI-generated videos on YouTube earlier this year.

items.title: AI breakthroughs in robotics won’t change your life any time soon
items.summary: While tech leaders like Elon Musk predict a near-future revolution in humanoid robotics, many researchers remain skeptical that current AI models can master the complexities of the physical world. The industry faces a significant gap between the hype surrounding human-like robots and the technical reality of achieving true physical dexterity.
items.content:
The story is a collaboration between MIT Technology Review and Aventine, a non-profit research foundation that creates and supports content about how technology and science are changing the way we live.

A robot shaped like a human—white with a black head and torso—has been popping up on video feeds. Perhaps you’ve seen it dance or pass popcorn, put trash in a bin, vacuum, or press the button of a microwave. Or maybe you’ve watched it fall backward while handing out water bottles or struggle to iron a shirt. 

This would be Tesla’s Optimus, an AI-powered humanoid robot that Elon Musk, the company’s CEO, believes will be “not just Tesla’s biggest product ever, but probably the biggest product ever,” headed to work on factory floors and, later, in our homes. Eventually it “will have human and then superhuman dexterity,” he told shareholders in July. Optimus robots could automate almost all human labor—from hauling sheet metal to folding laundry—for as little as $20,000 each, Musk argues. Speaking at the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Davos, Switzerland, in January, he predicted they could be on sale to the public by the end of 2027.

Musk is not alone in his evangelism. Marc Andreessen, cofounder and general partner of the Silicon Valley venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, has said that robotics could become the “biggest industry in the history of the planet.” In January, Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, said that humanoid robots would match human-level ability this year. According to Morgan Stanley, the number of robots that “resemble and act like humans” is likely to reach nearly 1 billion by 2050, creating a market worth over $5 trillion. 

Elon Musk predicts that Tesla’s Optimus humanoid could be one the world’s best-selling products. For now, it’s most often seen handing out food and drinks at Tesla events.SIPA VIA AP IMAGES

Such proclamations are in large part fueled by the idea that the same AI advances behind tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude will enable a new generation of robots to imitate human movement the way chatbots imitate human language. But many robotics researchers are skeptical, arguing that such assumptions minimize the challenges of using an intelligence built on language and images to master the infinite variability of the physical world. “None of those companies [building humanoid robots]—absolutely none of them—has any idea how to make those robots smart enough to be useful,” Yann LeCun, often referred to as one of the godfathers of AI, said at another event during the January Davos conference.  

Researchers also point out that the tendency to conflate humanoid robots made to resemble people with so-called generalist machines able to learn and perform multiple tasks is misleading. ”It’s very easy to make a robot that looks like a person,” explains Jonathan Hurst, cofounder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics and professor of robotics at Oregon State University. “It is dramatically more difficult to make a machine that moves or behaves dynamically or physically like a person.”  

These tensions—over whether all-purpose humanoid robots are just around the corner or nowhere in sight, and whether current forms of AI are all that’s needed to perfect them—are playing out in robotics labs across the country, where the hype over timelines is obscuring painstaking but meaningful progress.

A decade or so ago, a series of breakthroughs led to a generative AI revolution that turned the long-imagined possibility of artificial intelligence into reality. Roboticists—though they disagree on exactly when this will happen—believe that an equally transformative revolution is possible in robotics, one that will endow machines with physical intuition and fluidity that has long been out of reach. As progress in robotics inches forward, the question is whether the same methods and tools that fueled advances in AI are enough to get there, or if an entirely new path is required.

Robots meet advanced AI

To see one of the smartest robot brains working today, it’s worth looking at what Google DeepMind can do with a piece of equipment called ALOHA 2, short for “A Low-cost Open-source Hardware System for Bimanual Teleoperation.” 

Roboticists have long clashed over whether a humanlike form is necessary for generalist robots, with proponents arguing that it will help them slot into the world as it exists and detractors saying it’s not worth the trouble. ALOHA 2 reflects this second way of thinking. Not much to look at, it’s just a pair of arms, some grippers, and a couple of cameras. But despite its seeming simplicity, it is a workhorse for researchers at Google DeepMind, who use it to test their most advanced AI for robotics system, Gemini Robotics, in their various labs.

When controlled by Gemini Robotics, ALOHA 2 becomes more of a generalist robot, in the sense that it can perform any number of tasks based on examples it’s been trained on. Ask it to pack a lunchbox and, as evidenced by a video of this exercise, it can use two pincer grippers to delicately place a piece of white bread into a Ziploc bag, close it, place a bunch of grapes in a Tupperware container, secure the lid, and then carefully move the items into a lunchbox before zipping it up. 

It’s not a great lunch. But the fact that the robot can put it together represents an objective step forward from what was possible even, say, three years ago. 

This is in large part due to AI and its impact on what are known as robot policies, which controls how a general-purpose robot will need to assess and understand its surroundings, plan how to move within them, and then perform its task correctly.

The ALOHA 2 robot isn’t much more than two mechanical arms on a bench top, but it serves as a testbed for cutting-edge AI robotics models. items.title: Building a safer path to autonomous industrial AI
items.summary: Industrial AI is evolving toward autonomous physical systems, necessitating a focus on safety, governance, and human-in-the-loop oversight. Organizations must integrate data-driven insights with robust safeguards to ensure these technologies improve efficiency and sustainability without compromising critical infrastructure.
items.content:
Industrial AI is entering a new phase. After decades of predictive analytics and other specialized applications, advances in foundation models, physical AI, and agentic AI are making it possible to automate more complex tasks across industrial environments. But unlike AI that operates purely in the digital world, industrial AI can interact directly with physical systems, where an unexpected decision can have consequences for safety, reliability, and critical infrastructure.

That makes responsible deployment central to the next wave of industrial automation. “How do we leverage these technologies while maintaining safety, while maintaining reliable operations, while still being able to deliver on the promises of the new capabilities?” asks Arti Garg, chief technologist at AVEVA. The challenge is particularly acute as newer AI systems become more capable but also harder to predict and explain.

One foundation for making that transition work is data. Industrial systems often contain information across telemetry, service logs, engineering documents, and other disparate sources. Newer technologies can help connect and correlate that information more quickly, giving operators real-time support when diagnosing problems. AI-powered robots could take that a step further by gathering information in hazardous environments without requiring workers to enter them.

But greater autonomy also requires new approaches to governance. AVEVA’s framework for responsible AI emphasizes security, efficiency, and human safety and oversight. Garg argues that AI should augment rather than replace people in critical decision loops, with guardrails determining where automated systems can act and where human supervisors remain responsible.

Sustainability is another part of that equation. AI can help manage complex power systems as renewable generation grows, while organizations also need better ways to understand AI’s own environmental footprint. Garg is involved in an IEEE working group developing a standard methodology for measuring that impact across electricity, energy, resources, water, and carbon.

The next phase could bring industrial AI further into the physical world, from autonomous robots and drones to AI-assisted coding that allows domain experts to build new applications. But realizing that potential will require more than deploying new technology, says Garg. Organizations will need to rethink business processes, establish appropriate safeguards, and give experienced workers new ways to apply their expertise, creating a model of automation that is not only more autonomous, but safer, more efficient, and more sustainable.

“Autonomous systems, whether they’re robots or drones, are really going to change the way that we work in plants, in power systems, on mining sites,” says Garg. “In a way, that will make these types of operations more efficient, much safer for the human beings involved and more productive.”

This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with AVEVA.

Full Transcript

Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.

Industrial AI may not be new, but it is developing at a breakneck pace. From modern predictive analytics that can preempt equipment failures, to autonomous robots tasked with inspecting high risk machinery, emerging applications have the potential to transform operational efficiencies. But often used in high consequence environments with minimal margin for error, industrial AI deployed without clarity, security, or accountability could also have catastrophic consequences for critical infrastructure over time. As industries rush to embrace the latest technologies, the goal should always be responsible AI designed to support, rather than replace that all important human judgment.

Two words for you: sustainable automation.

My guest today is Arti Garg, chief technologist at AVEVA.

This podcast is produced in partnership with AVEVA.

Welcome, Arti.

Arti Garg: Thank you, Megan. It’s great to be here.

Megan: Thank you so much for joining us. And just to start, if we could set some context for our discussion, can you share a bit about the current state of industrial AI and what AVEVA is working on at the moment as well?

Arti: Yeah, more than happy to. And I want to go back to what you already stated, which is that in some ways, industrial AI is not new. It’s something that, even here at AVEVA, we’ve been working on for more than 20 years, really thinking about how AI can enhance applications in the industrial sector.

But what has changed quite substantially in maybe the last few years is the type of AI. We’ve really moved to these general purpose foundation models, which enable a lot more people to leverage advanced AI technologies. In addition to that, in just the last couple of years, there’s been an explosion in what’s known as physical AI and the types of AI that can really accelerate the capabilities of robotics and autonomous systems. And also agentic AI, which also allows for automation at more of the software level.

And what we’re seeing is that while in the past there has been some hesitancy to adopt models that don’t totally have predictable outcomes, there’s been a rapid acceleration in adoption of AI even in the industrial sector. One study suggests maybe that’s almost a 78% increase over the past just two years within the industrial sector. So yes, that’s an inflection point, but it’s almost like a step function if you think about it with respect to AI adoption.

And what we’re really thinking about now at AVEVA is, how do we think about this? How do we think about incorporating these new and very powerful AI technologies in environments where customers have mission-critical operations, human safety is a significant factor? Those are some of the primary concerns that our customers have when they think a

items.title: Anthropic gives outside AI watchdog “employee-like” access
items.summary: Anthropic has granted the nonprofit watchdog METR employee-like access to its internal systems and hardware to evaluate potential AI risks. This move reflects a growing industry trend of using third-party oversight to address safety concerns regarding advanced artificial intelligence.
items.content:
Anthropic has granted external evaluators “employee-like access” to assess the risks of its models, following through on a commitment to increase safeguards over concerns the technology could run catastrophically out of control.

METR, a nonprofit that has worked with leading labs including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, now has a team embedded in the Claude maker’s office with access to its hardware and internal systems.

A greater role for third-party evaluators is among the main concrete steps the labs have proposed in response to rising concern about the dangers more capable AI systems could pose to the economy, cyber security and humanity at large.

items.title: Accused OpenAI spy had folder called “Saudi Gov Docs,” FBI says
items.summary: A former OpenAI engineer remains in custody after being accused of planting bugs to steal company secrets. Prosecutors allege the suspect may have been acting on behalf of the Saudi Arabian government.
items.content:
On Monday, a court granted the US government's request to deny release of a former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a top-secret conference room to steal the frontier lab’s secrets.

In a court filing Sunday, US attorney Craig Missakian argued that Abdulrahman Alfozan must continue to be detained while the US makes its case that Alfozan brazenly spied on OpenAI, either for his own personal business gain or to benefit the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

Evidence showed that Alfozan had been chatting with a member of the KSA royal family on WhatsApp, while pursuing opportunities to permanently move back to Saudi Arabia during the country's biggest AI push yet, the government argued. Shortly before his arrest, the FBI found he accessed a folder called "Saudi Gov Docs" on his iPhone, where he also allegedly stored photos of a second bug he planted in the offices.
