items.summary: Software engineers are expressing growing discomfort with the industry shift toward shipping AI-generated code that they do not fully understand. Professionals are debating whether to adapt by relying on rigorous automated testing, documentation, and architectural oversight to maintain system integrity.
items.content:
|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  | **[Hacker News](news)**[new](newest) | [past](front) | [comments](newcomments) | <ask> | <show> | <jobs> | <submit> | [login](login?goto=item%3Fid%3D50151036) | |
|
| |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?](item?id=50151036) | |  | | 14 points by [rzk](user?id=rzk) [5 hours ago](item?id=50151036)  | [hide](hide?id=50151036&goto=item%3Fid%3D50151036) | [past](https://hn.algolia.com/?query=Ask%20HN%3A%20How%20to%20deal%20with%20shipping%20AI-written%20code%20you%20don%27t%20understand%3F&type=story&dateRange=all&sort=byDate&storyText=false&prefix&page=0) | [favorite](fave?id=50151036) | [24 comments](item?id=50151036) | |  | | I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie\_im-an-engineer-at-meta-and-i-never-felt-share-7517317918666211328-7C8N > I'm an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doing my job. I'm writing code these days and it all feels like a black box. This new standard of shipping with AI is moving so fast that if we're going to spend our time checking each line of code, it's going to take forever. That means you can end up with systems you've built where you don't truly understand how all the code works. You understand the high level, but not every detail. And maybe this is becoming the new standard. It goes against every instinct of being a software engineer. I'm used to understanding what I'm building. Now I'm trying to figure out how much I need to understand before I'm comfortable moving forward. Are other engineers feeling this too? How are you handling this? | | |  | | [help](formatdoc) |     |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [webarchitect](user?id=webarchitect) [21 minutes ago](item?id=50154869)  | [next](#50154019) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   I can think of so many times this has happened before. People getting used to MVC, Dependency Injection, ORMs. Sometimes the code is so large you only work on a part of it, so you have to get used to a lot of not knowing. So how do we build confidence anyhow when we can't know everything? I think first, standard checks - does it compile? What do static analysis tools say - code quality, passes SAST analysis? Linters? Style checkers? Do the tests run? I'm not comfortable with the tests I write let alone the AI.. by adding fault injection (fuzzing, chaos), and mutation testing, I have a better degree of confidence in the tests and code. Spend even more time getting to know the product instead. Maybe I don't know the code as well as I used to, but I know the product backwards and forwards. That helps me have some new confidence that I didn't really have before. Knowing the greater whole.  [reply](reply?id=50154869&goto=item%3Fid%3D50151036%2350154869) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [lp92](user?id=lp92) [1 hour ago](item?id=50154019)  | [prev](#50154869) | [next](#50151443) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   I'm currently working on a combined Aero sim/CAD/CAM software for designing, simulating, and performing DFM optimization specifically for Group 1 to 3 winged UAVs. What I do is ask Opus/Gemini to explain the parts I don't understand. And I do some of my own research to verify accuracy of the explanations. In addition: \* Every new feature has a Feature Design document which I review, modify, and approve. And a corresponding Implementation Plan which I also review and approve. \* Every fix has a RCA document and fix Implementation Doc which I review, modify, and approve. \* There's a global high level Architecture and Design document with additional sub component design documents which are always kept in synch after a new feature or bug fix is done. Synching it is always a step in the Implementation plan. This does adds some overhead but it allows me to have have check point gates. This has often allowed me to catch misunderstandings and align properly before any code gets edited by the AI agent. Having the above docs also helps when it comes to referencing them as context to properly ground new features or bug fixes.  [reply](reply?id=50154019&goto=item%3Fid%3D50151036%2350154019) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [pinscope\_dev](user?id=pinscope_dev) [5 hours ago](item?id=50151443)  | [prev](#50154019) | [next](#50153483) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   I had same problem, but after a while I just accepted that is inevitable  [reply](reply?id=50151443&goto=item%3Fid%3D50151036%2350151443) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [polski-g](user?id=polski-g) [3 hours ago](item?id=50152554)  | [parent](#50151443) | [next](#50153483) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   "This code is really ugly." That sucks. Ship it.  [reply](reply?id=50152554&goto=item%3Fid%3D50151036%2350152554) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [benfidge](user?id=benfidge) [2 hours ago](item?id=50153483)  | [prev](#50151443) | [next](#50152868) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Generally speaking I brain storm the feature first and produce a dev plan. This includes asking it to reuse code/libraries we’ve already got! After it’s gone off ah done its thing we go back over and do a QA on what it’s built, why that approach, what can we do better etc etc?  [reply](reply?id=50153483&goto=item%3Fid%3D50151036%2350153483) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [sdevonoes](user?id=sdevonoes) [3 hours ago](item?id=50152868)  | [prev](#50153483) | [next](#50152829) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Product doesn’t care. And most of us will get replaced by agents. I guess around 30% of the engineering workforce will keep their jobs which will be mainly to keep the product up and running, doing whatever it takes (so using agents to fix stuff basically). The ones who get to keep their jobs will be rebranded as Maintenance engineers with a lower salary. VPs and Heads of will keep their cozy job (bc there are not so many of them), and they are not that dumb to fire themselves. Code understanding doesn’t matter anymore (or won’t matter soon)  [reply](reply?id=50152868&goto=item%3Fid%3D50151036%2350152868) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [billylo](user?id=billylo) [3 hours ago](item?id=50152829)  | [prev](#50152868) | [next](#50151160) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   I spend time to add extra observability, cross-checking and alerting at runtime to offset the risk.  [reply](reply?id=50152829&goto=item%3Fid%3D50151036%2350152829) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [spacedcowboy](user?id=spacedcowboy) [5 hours ago](item?id=50151160)  | [prev](#50152829) | [next](#50151085) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   I’m slowly coming around to the idea that if it works, I’m good with that. I never used to personally check all my colleagues work, either, I just trusted that they’d done a good job. That’s not to say I blindly trust an LLM - my project is an autovectorising compiler. I have it write a bazillion tests, and I have real, non-trivial programs that it compiled. I have it run a ‘gate’ before releases that takes literally hours on 5 different architectures. To say this code is tested is … masterful understatement. I think what helps is a long planning session, going into details, working out corner cases, designing test-cases, you know work and effort. Once that’s done it’s easier to let it work through the night and do a major production feature. I still review the code, but hand on heart I couldn’t say I’d reviewed *everything*, sometimes I miss something in a complicated check-in. I try to keep checkins small and contained, but sometimes that’s not easy to manage alongside the “don’t break stuff” rule as well. So it comes down to: I’ve been working on this for 6 months or so, and so far this has worked out for me. You know, kind of like getting used to a colleague’s idiosyncrasies over a period of time. I will say that in my experience the code quality is fairly high. Maybe that’s down to the effort put in ahead of time in the planning stages, I don’t know, but I don’t seem to suffer from the ‘slop’ that people complain of. YMMV.  [reply](reply?id=50151160&goto=item%3Fid%3D50151036%2350151160) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [yulaow](user?id=yulaow) [5 hours ago](item?id=50151337)  | [parent](#50151160) | [next](#50151085) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   I am not in META but for what I read on blind, assuming it is true, they are not spending any time in long planning sessions or in getting into details of the implementation plan at all, and they could not anymore considering how many PRs in parallel they are requested to manage  [reply](reply?id=50151337&goto=item%3Fid%3D50151036%2350151337) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [spacedcowboy](user?id=spacedcowboy) [4 hours ago](item?id=50151734)  | [root](#50151160) | [parent](#50151337) | [next](#50151085) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Yeah, I'm retired. The only person I have to answer to regarding progress is me. I'm a stubborn son of a bitch when it comes to choosing quality over speed... That doesn't mean I don't like progress mind :) This morning I got the preliminary results of a 'C' front-end to the compiler (it uses clang to compile to LLVM IR, then translates to our IR, then feeds that IR into the autovectoriser as if it had parsed the code itself). So for *the exact same source code* I now have: ```      ┌─────────────┬────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────┐      │  Benchmark  │ clang -O2  │ xcc --par-auto (GPU) │ Speed-up │      ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤      │ saxpy       │ 1,546 µs   │ 726 µs               │ 2.1×     │      ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤      │ Mandelbrot  │ 394,238 µs │ 2,110 µs             │ 187×     │      ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤      │ nbody       │ 37,090 µs  │ 1,035 µs             │ 36×      │      ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤      │ perlin      │ 78,016 µs  │ 1,850 µs             │ 42×      │      ├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤      │ mandel_deep │ 73.2 s     │ 55.8 ms              │ 1,312×   │      └─────────────┴────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────┘  ```  Those are some pretty fine speedups, from naive C, with *no alterations* from the standard "C" code - it automatically finds places that can be made data-parallel, tracks the data-hazards to make sure its safe to "GPU" and writes all the kernels, boilerplate and data-stream-management if necessary. Obviously the checksums have to match, so I know it did the work correctly too :) Hacker News isn't interested - any post I make linking to the webpages is immediately blocked/dead so I'll wait until the C++ front-end is ready (some time next week) and announce it somewhere else. A compiler that takes standard C/C++ code and speeds it up by automatically finding data-parallel areas and scheduling them on the GPU with no programming overhead is pretty rare. Oh, and it manages the local network as well, so you can run xcd on machines on your lan, or via the TB4/5 bridge between Macs and it'll schedule on other GPUs, just like it manages multiple GPUs on the local machine. It characterises both latency and compute-time to figure out which devices are worth scheduling on. items.summary: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has issued an order banning federal civilian agencies from using DeepSeek AI models due to national security and data privacy concerns. The directive prohibits the use of DeepSeek technology even when hosted locally, citing risks of data transfer to China and potential vulnerabilities within the models.
items.content:
|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  | **[Hacker News](news)**[new](newest) | [past](front) | [comments](newcomments) | <ask> | <show> | <jobs> | <submit> | [login](login?goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244) | |
|
| |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [DeepSeek banned from U.S. federal civilian agencies under new DHS order](https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-21447.pdf) ([federalregister.gov](from?site=federalregister.gov)) | |  | | 30 points by [cmrdporcupine](user?id=cmrdporcupine) [6 hours ago](item?id=50154244)  | [hide](hide?id=50154244&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244) | [past](https://hn.algolia.com/?query=DeepSeek%20banned%20from%20U.S.%20federal%20civilian%20agencies%20under%20new%20DHS%20order&type=story&dateRange=all&sort=byDate&storyText=false&prefix&page=0) | [favorite](fave?id=50154244) | [12 comments](item?id=50154244) | |  | |  | | |  | | [help](formatdoc) |     |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [gavinray](user?id=gavinray) [6 hours ago](item?id=50154282)  | [next](#50156170) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Here's the transcription of the reasoning: ```   > Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co., Ltd. (hereinafter DeepSeek), a foreign, privately-owned company, located in the People’s Republic of China (PRC) provides multiple artificial intelligence applications available widely and free of charge. DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors. DeepSeek servers are located in the PRC, and the PRC legal system permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure. For DeepSeek-hosted instances of their models, DeepSeek’s account generation process collects personally identifiable information (PII) and may also track and digitally fingerprint users. DeepSeek’s most widely used applications function through a prompt-and-response process that requires presenting information to the model, and which may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC if used by U.S. government employees or vendors. The transfer of the aforementioned information to the PRC, either independently or in combination with publicly available data, could produce actionable intelligence on U.S. persons and/or government programs. The models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities. Indeed, open-source security research has found that the DeepSeek iOS mobile application contains multiple critical vulnerabilities. ```  [reply](reply?id=50154282&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350154282) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [cmrdporcupine](user?id=cmrdporcupine) [6 hours ago](item?id=50154345)  | [parent](#50154282) | [next](#50156170) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Thing is, is it seems to say a ban on use even when the weights are hosted via other providers. *"third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations"* So you could be hosting it fully locally inside the agency and still it would be banned. It's not *surprising* to me, but it's pretty blunt. Not that I care what US agencies do, but this does seem like the first step of many to come.  [reply](reply?id=50154345&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350154345) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [tmp10423288442](user?id=tmp10423288442) [4 hours ago](item?id=50155788)  | [root](#50154282) | [parent](#50154345) | [next](#50156170) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   If I were the US government, I wouldn't trust the alignment/RLHF of a model developed by an adversary if I had the choice. Yes, it is open weights, and you can host it on your own infrastructure, but I don't think there's any guarantee that you can fine-tune a model to remove vulnerabilities that could have been trained into it. I realize that non-US nations could ask the same about the US. All I will say is that there are consequences to failing to nurture a competitive tech industry - even Mistral is basing their newest models on China open-weights models. Unlike the EU, the US government is fortunate to have a choice.  [reply](reply?id=50155788&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350155788) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [jacquesm](user?id=jacquesm) [4 hours ago](item?id=50156170)  | [prev](#50154282) | [next](#50155543) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   The models may well contain malware or security vulnerabilities. But they are at least open to inspection because the weights are available, the same can not be said about US providers of inference such as OpenAI and Anthropic.  [reply](reply?id=50156170&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350156170) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [cmrdporcupine](user?id=cmrdporcupine) [3 hours ago](item?id=50156525)  | [parent](#50156170) | [next](#50155543) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   It's also odd for them to single out DeepSeek in particular, and not just any model from the PRC?  [reply](reply?id=50156525&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350156525) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [jacquesm](user?id=jacquesm) [3 hours ago](item?id=50156551)  | [root](#50156170) | [parent](#50156525) | [next](#50155543) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   DeepSeek is the one that is the most visible, and probably the most cited in the departure messages to US providers.  [reply](reply?id=50156551&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350156551) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [johnnyApplePRNG](user?id=johnnyApplePRNG) [4 hours ago](item?id=50155543)  | [prev](#50156170) | [next](#50157291) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Deepseek V4.1 Flash 1017 is out of this world good ... and cheap ... that's why.  [reply](reply?id=50155543&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350155543) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [GlickWick](user?id=GlickWick) [2 hours ago](item?id=50157405)  | [parent](#50155543) | [next](#50157291) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   That's not why. We've entered a pretty adversarial era, and we know there are unexpected attack vectors available in frontier models. Just because you an inspect the weights doesn't mean you can derive the behavior. I suspect the CCP would ban US models if they didn't need to distill them to make their own.  [reply](reply?id=50157405&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350157405) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [tmp10423288442](user?id=tmp10423288442) [1 hour ago](item?id=50158507)  | [root](#50155543) | [parent](#50157405) | [next](#50157291) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   > I suspect the CCP would ban US models if they didn't need to distill them to make their own. I'm pretty sure they do, at least officially. But obviously the distillation and API proxies used by Chinese uses are unofficially tolerated and even exploited.  [reply](reply?id=50158507&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350158507) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [sciencesama](user?id=sciencesama) [2 hours ago](item?id=50157291)  | [prev](#50155543) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   how can an open source model be banned ?  [reply](reply?id=50157291&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350157291) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [GlickWick](user?id=GlickWick) [2 hours ago](item?id=50157391)  | [parent](#50157291) | [next](#50158734) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Easily? Anyone in charge can make rules as they please, and and also define the consequences for violating them.  [reply](reply?id=50157391&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350157391) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [sekh60](user?id=sekh60) [38 minutes ago](item?id=50158734)  | [parent](#50157291) | [prev](#50157391) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Open weight.  [reply](reply?id=50158734&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154244%2350158734) | | |

items.summary: Electronic Arts is shutting down the video game studio BioWare. The announcement has sparked discussion on Hacker News regarding the studio's legacy and the broader trend of corporate acquisitions in the gaming industry.
items.content:
|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  | **[Hacker News](news)**[new](newest) | [past](front) | [comments](newcomments) | <ask> | <show> | <jobs> | <submit> | [login](login?goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586) | |
|
| |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [EA is shutting down BioWare](https://www.theverge.com/games/1015647/ea-is-shutting-down-bioware) ([theverge.com](from?site=theverge.com)) | |  | | 54 points by [aaronbrethorst](user?id=aaronbrethorst) [41 minutes ago](item?id=50184586)  | [hide](hide?id=50184586&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586) | [past](https://hn.algolia.com/?query=EA%20is%20shutting%20down%20BioWare&type=story&dateRange=all&sort=byDate&storyText=false&prefix&page=0) | [favorite](fave?id=50184586) | [19 comments](item?id=50184586) | |  | |  | | |  | | [help](formatdoc) |     |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [everdrive](user?id=everdrive) [13 minutes ago](item?id=50185007)  | [next](#50185120) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   It's the new hot business model. Buy a very successful studio then liquidate it.  [reply](reply?id=50185007&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185007) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [jbmchuck](user?id=jbmchuck) [1 minute ago](item?id=50185152)  | [parent](#50185007) | [next](#50185067) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Nothing new under the sun - [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embrace,\_extend,\_and\_extinguis...](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embrace,_extend,_and_extinguish)  [reply](reply?id=50185152&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185152) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [mosura](user?id=mosura) [8 minutes ago](item?id=50185067)  | [parent](#50185007) | [prev](#50185152) | [next](#50185060) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Bioware have not been very successful for a very long time. Even in the good times their ability to create (and hide) black holes was prodigious.  [reply](reply?id=50185067&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185067) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [HelloMcFly](user?id=HelloMcFly) [8 minutes ago](item?id=50185060)  | [parent](#50185007) | [prev](#50185067) | [next](#50185120) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Bioware hasn't been very successful - creatively or economically - in some time. I loved their heyday more than most, but they're far from what they once were.  [reply](reply?id=50185060&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185060) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [kobalsky](user?id=kobalsky) [3 minutes ago](item?id=50185120)  | [prev](#50185007) | [next](#50185043) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Talent in western game studios just can't shake the startup mode. Try get a hit, try to get bought, cash out, run away. Blizzard seemed to defy the stereotype but it died a long time ago, it's just a husk. The contrast with japanese game studios is impressive.  [reply](reply?id=50185120&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185120) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [loosescrews](user?id=loosescrews) [0 minutes ago](item?id=50185162)  | [parent](#50185120) | [next](#50185043) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Bioware had a string of hits before EA bought them.  [reply](reply?id=50185162&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185162) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [WithinReason](user?id=WithinReason) [9 minutes ago](item?id=50185043)  | [prev](#50185120) | [next](#50185122) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   The makers of Baldur's Gate, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Neverwinter Nights, Mass Effect, Dragon Age: Origins. Sad, even though BioWare was dead already.  [reply](reply?id=50185043&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185043) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [LarsDu88](user?id=LarsDu88) [4 minutes ago](item?id=50185101)  | [parent](#50185043) | [next](#50185122) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Let us not forget MDK2  [reply](reply?id=50185101&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185101) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [Mr\_Eri\_Atlov](user?id=Mr_Eri_Atlov) [3 minutes ago](item?id=50185122)  | [prev](#50185043) | [next](#50184939) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Knights of the Old Republic will forever be one of my favorite games RIP to an amazing creative group  [reply](reply?id=50185122&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185122) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [ndesaulniers](user?id=ndesaulniers) [18 minutes ago](item?id=50184939)  | [prev](#50185122) | [next](#50184989) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Many great memories of KOTOR, Jade Empire, Mass Effect. RIP  [reply](reply?id=50184939&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350184939) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [barbazoo](user?id=barbazoo) [14 minutes ago](item?id=50184989)  | [prev](#50184939) | [next](#50184933) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   > The company is also laying off around 400 staffers, Bloomberg reports, including around 50 at BioWare. The changes follow EA being taken private by an investor group led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners in a $55 billion deal that closed in August. Never thought that Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund would shutdown the company that created so many childhood memories.  [reply](reply?id=50184989&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350184989) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [glimshe](user?id=glimshe) [18 minutes ago](item?id=50184933)  | [prev](#50184989) | [next](#50185047) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   One of my favorite game companies ever. But it had already been "shut down" in practice after the acquisition.  [reply](reply?id=50184933&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350184933) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [eterm](user?id=eterm) [9 minutes ago](item?id=50185054)  | [parent](#50184933) | [next](#50185047) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Yes, the mourning for the company that made KOTOR and NWN was done years ago, it's effectively a completely different company now that's shutting down.  [reply](reply?id=50185054&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185054) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [seattle\_spring](user?id=seattle_spring) [9 minutes ago](item?id=50185047)  | [prev](#50184933) | [next](#50184999) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   End of an era, but the writing has been on the wall for a while now.  [reply](reply?id=50185047&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185047) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [bluefirebrand](user?id=bluefirebrand) [13 minutes ago](item?id=50184999)  | [prev](#50185047) | [next](#50184983) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Bioware hasn't released a good game in over a decade, and Anthem was a low point for the entire game industry imo I'm honestly surprised they lasted this long. Sad to see them go but only because they should have been way better  [reply](reply?id=50184999&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350184999) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [indy](user?id=indy) [9 minutes ago](item?id=50185049)  | [parent](#50184999) | [next](#50184983) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Exactly, the Bioware that people love hasn't existed for a long time  [reply](reply?id=50185049&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185049) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [2OEH8eoCRo0](user?id=2OEH8eoCRo0) [14 minutes ago](item?id=50184983)  | [prev](#50184999) | [next](#50184982) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   The studio behind masterpieces like Dragon Age Veilguard and Mass Effect Andromeda? Sad day  [reply](reply?id=50184983&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350184983) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [baal80spam](user?id=baal80spam) [7 minutes ago](item?id=50185079)  | [parent](#50184983) | [next](#50184982) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   You forgot /s, right? Anyway - good riddance.  [reply](reply?id=50185079&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350185079) | | | |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | |  |  | [r0ckarong](user?id=r0ckarong) [15 minutes ago](item?id=50184982)  | [prev](#50184983) [[–]](javascript:void(0))   Another victim of EA. Bought, ruined, buried.  [reply](reply?id=50184982&goto=item%3Fid%3D50184586%2350184982) | | |

items.title: OpenAI Nears Launch of AI Agent Tool to Automate Tasks for Users
items.summary: OpenAI plans to launch an AI agent codenamed Operator in January that can autonomously perform multi-step computer tasks for users. This release marks a broader industry shift toward agentic software as companies seek new breakthroughs beyond traditional model development.
items.content: (Bloomberg) -- OpenAI is preparing to launch a new artificial intelligence agent codenamed "Operator" that can use a computer to take actions on a person's behalf, such as writing code or booking travel, according to two people familiar with the matter. In a staff meeting on Wednesday, OpenAI's leadership announced plans to release the tool in January as a research preview and through the company's application programming interface for developers, said one of the people, who spoke on the [...] The planned release is part of a broader industry push toward agents, or AI software that can complete multi-step tasks for users with minimal supervision. Anthropic unveiled a similar agent that can process what's happening on the user's computer in real time and take actions on their behalf. OpenAI-backer Microsoft Corp. also recently launched a set of agent tools designed to send emails and manage records for workers. And Alphabet Inc.'s Google is said to be preparing to release an AI agent, [...] the thing that will feel like the next giant breakthrough will be agents."The move to release an agentic AI tool also comes as OpenAI and its competitors have seen diminishing returns from their costly efforts to develop more advanced AI models.

items.title: OpenAI launches new tools to help businesses build AI agents | TechCrunch
items.summary: OpenAI has launched the Responses API and an open-source Agents SDK to help businesses build and manage autonomous AI agents. These new tools will eventually replace the existing Assistants API as the company shifts focus toward more advanced agentic workflows.
items.content: On Tuesday, OpenAI released new tools designed to help developers and enterprises build AI agents — automated systems that can independently accomplish tasks — using the company’s own AI models and frameworks. [...] Alongside the Responses API, OpenAI is releasing an open-source toolkit called the Agents SDK, which offers developers free tools to integrate models with their internal systems, put in place safeguards, and monitor AI agent activities for debugging and optimization purposes. The Agents SDK is a follow-up of sorts to OpenAI’s Swarm, a framework for multi-agent orchestration that the company released late last year. [...] The tools are part of OpenAI’s new Responses API, which lets businesses develop custom AI agents that can perform web searches, scan through company files, and navigate websites, much like OpenAI’s Operator product. The Responses API effectively replaces OpenAI’s Assistants API, which the company plans to sunset in the first half of 2026.

items.content: Zapier brings its established automation infrastructure to agentic AI with a builder that connects agents to more than 7,000 third-party applications out of the box—more native connectors than any other tool on this list. For teams already running Zapier automations, it's a quick jump to AI agents: existing Zaps become available as agent tools with minimal ramp-up. Though advanced observability and multi-agent capabilities are less developed than purpose-built agent platforms, for [...] AI agent tools are platforms, frameworks, and applications that enable autonomous AI systems to plan, decide, and act across workflows without requiring a human prompt for every step. Unlike traditional automation, which follows rigid rules, AI agent tools reason through ambiguous goals, use other tools in a tech stack, and adapt based on the results. AI agent tools is a broad category, spanning developer frameworks that give engineering teams full architectural control to enterprise platforms [...] CrewAI is a multi-agent orchestration framework that lets teams define agents with specific roles and goals, then coordinate them toward shared tasks—for example, a research agent surfaces information, a writer drafts, a reviewer evaluates. The crew-based design model is intuitive enough that teams can build complex multi-agent workflows without the architectural expertise that more flexible frameworks would demand. # OpenAI's agent tool may be nearing release

Kyle Wiggers

3 min read

OpenAI may be close to releasing an AI tool that can take control of your PC and perform actions on your behalf. [...] OpenAI's imminent entry into the AI agent space comes as rivals, including the aforementioned Anthropic, Google, and others, make plays for the nascent segment. AI agents may be risky and speculative, but tech giants are already touting them as the next big thing in AI. According to analytics firm Markets and Markets, the market for AI agents could be worth $47.1 billion by 2030. [...] According to The Information, OpenAI is targeting January as Operator's release month. Code uncovered by Blaho this weekend adds credence to that reporting.

items.title: AI Agent Change Management and Release Controls | GS
items.summary: AI agent change management requires governing the entire decision system rather than just individual prompts or models. Safe releases must include bounded authority, rigorous testing, controlled rollouts, and verified rollback procedures.
items.content:
Trace the change in both directions. A new tool can require new permissions, logs, tests, alerts, approvals, and incident steps. A new model can alter tool selection, refusal, output shape, cost, latency, and evaluation validity. A new retrieval filter can change source coverage and which protected data enters the task. [...] Restoring code does not remove a poisoned memory, queued retry, changed permission, sent message, or modified downstream record.

AI agent change management must govern the full decision system. A safe release is not a new prompt or model in production. It is an approved version set with bounded authority, representative test proof, a controlled rollout, a real rollback path, and evidence that the system behaved as expected. [...] GS Agent Change Release Impact Index ranking twelve AI agent change classes 

Tools and action schemas lead, followed by orchestration, approval policy, identity, credential gateways, memory, retrieval, model, instruction, evaluation, and monitoring changes.

Tuesday's announcement was not the long-rumored ChatGPT-5, which could arrive as soon as this week. Instead, the new model is OpenAI's first open-weight language model since the release of GPT-2 in 2019.

"As part of this, we are quite hopeful that this release will enable new kinds of research and the creation of new kinds of products," Altman wrote. "We expect a meaningful uptick in the rate of innovation in our field, and for many more people to do important work than were able to before." [...] OpenAI's AI models are getting more open. At least, some of them are.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman announced GPT-oss on Tuesday, an "open" family of language models with "open weights" that the CEO said can operate locally on a "high-end laptop" and smartphones.

An AI model with "open weights" is one whose fully trained parameter weights are made publicly downloadable, so anyone can run, inspect, or fine-tune the AI model locally. [...] Altman had previously signaled that OpenAI would return to releasing at least some open model, saying that, "We're going to do a very powerful open source model" that was "better than any current open source model out there."

Meta has long published the open weights of its LLAMA AI models.

A weight release means a user can retrieve the checkpoint files under a visible license. This tracker records the event that made a model downloadable and keeps announcement dates separate when they differ.

 

### How should a team evaluate a new open-weight LLM? [...] ### KAT-Coder-V2.5-Dev Is a Coding Derivative

KAT-Coder-V2.5-Dev is a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters and an Apache-2.0 checkpoint.

Its card states that this open-weight release contains only the language-model weights, not the vision components. Runtime flags may need to disable multimodal initialization.

That is the kind of deployment detail a release tracker should surface. A successful download is not the same as a successful server start.

items.title: How Open-Weight Models Changed the AI Landscape
items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts transformer architectures have become the standard foundation for frontier open-weight LLMs. These models utilize stacked blocks consisting of attention and feed-forward layers to process information efficiently.
items.content:
Every major open-weight LLM released at the frontier in 2025 and 2026 shares the same architectural skeleton. It is called a Mixture-of-Experts transformer, or MoE for short.

Modern LLMs are built from stacked “blocks.” Each block has two main parts, an attention layer that figures out which previous words matter for the next one, and a feed-forward layer that does the actual computation.

items.summary: The article clarifies the distinction between open-source and open-weight LLMs while highlighting top performers like DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Kimi K2.6. It also introduces Onyx as a platform designed to help organizations operationalize and manage these models.
items.content:
### What is the difference between open-source and open-weight LLMs?

Open-source LLMs have publicly available weights, architecture, and (ideally) training code under a permissive license like MIT or Apache 2.0. Open-weight models release weights but may have proprietary training code or restrictive license terms. In practice, most "open-source" LLMs are open-weight: you can download and run them, but full source code and training data are rarely published. [...] Recommendation: Choose DeepSeek-V4-Pro when you want the strongest open-weight combination of software-engineering and code-generation performance under a fully permissive license.

### 2. Kimi K2.6 (Moonshot, Modified MIT)

Facts: Kimi K2.6 is listed under a Modified MIT license with 1T total / 32B active parameters, 80.2% SWE-bench, 90.5% GPQA Diamond, 89.6% LiveCodeBench, 83.2% BrowseComp, 73.1% OSWorld, 66.7% Terminal-Bench 2.0, and costs $0.95 / $4 per 1M input/output tokens. [...] ## What Is Onyx?

Onyx is an open-source AI platform that helps teams operationalize open-source and open-weight LLMs. The model provides inference, while Onyx supplies connectors, permission-aware retrieval, AI chat, agents, deep research, and user access across the organization.
